hook.text: Not all galaxies fit neat categories. Irregular galaxies have chaotic shapes with no clear structure.

buildup.text: They make up about 20% of galaxies. Most are small and rich in gas, fueling active star formation.

discovery.text: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are irregular galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, visible from the Southern Hemisphere.

twist.text: Many irregular galaxies were once spirals or ellipticals—distorted by gravitational encounters with larger neighbors.

climax.text: Irregular galaxies were more common in the early universe, when collisions and mergers happened frequently.

punchline.text: No arms, no bulge, no rules. Cosmic chaos at its most creative.

quiz.question: What causes many irregular galaxies to lose their original shape?
options: Gravitational interactions with larger neighboring galaxies
Rapid rotation that tears apart their spiral arms
Dark energy pushing their stars apart

details.summary: Irregular galaxies lack the organized structure of spirals or ellipticals — they appear chaotic, asymmetric, and clumpy. Many are rich in gas and display active star formation. They're often shaped by gravitational interactions with larger neighbors.
details.whyItMatters: Irregular galaxies often resemble the chaotic, gas-rich galaxies common in the early universe. Studying them provides insights into primordial galaxy conditions and the effects of gravitational interactions.
takeaways: Chaotic, asymmetric galaxies lacking organized structure
Often rich in gas with active star formation
Frequently shaped by interactions with larger neighbors

faq.question: What makes a galaxy irregular?
faq.answer: Gravitational interactions, tidal forces from nearby galaxies, or violent internal processes can disrupt organized structure. Some irregulars were once spirals distorted by a close encounter. Others may never have developed regular structure due to their small mass.

faq.question: Are the Magellanic Clouds being disrupted by the Milky Way?
faq.answer: Yes. The Milky Way's gravity is stretching them, producing the Magellanic Stream — a trail of hydrogen gas spanning 200 degrees across the sky. The Large Magellanic Cloud was once a barred spiral but has been distorted by tidal interactions. Both are expected to eventually merge with the Milky Way.
